title: Say what done means
about: Every line of code in this film is read from examples/plugged-in, and every line of terminal output is replayed from docs/manual/captures, recorded by running the commands for real.

lines.text: An agent can write a handler in minutes. So the question is never, can it build this. The question is, how will you know it's right.
The answer is to say what done means before anyone builds. And to have someone else say it.
In Orthograph, done is a journey: a short story, told through real calls to the real system.
One agent writes the journeys. We call it the author. A different agent builds until they pass, and it may not change them.
Here's the app we build across this series: Plugged In. A person claims a name, and gets a public page of links.
The stubs are made while planning, before anyone builds. The designer picks one thing: the handle.
And runs one command. ortho add journeys handle.
lines.say: And runs one command. Ortho, add journeys, handle.

lines.text: Seven files appear. One for each path through the handle's states, one for each role, and one for each error an operation declares.
Look inside one. A stranger tries to release a name that isn't theirs. The stub already knows who may call, and that this caller must be refused.
What it can't know, it leaves blank. And ortho check lists every blank as a question, with its file and its line.
lines.say: What it can't know, it leaves blank. And ortho check lists every blank as a question, with its file and its line.

scenes.title: A journey reads as a story

lines.text: The author fills the blanks, and writes the stories the stubs couldn't guess. This is the one you read.
Claim a handle. Eight steps, and each one is a sentence. A name nobody has claimed does not resolve. Aaron claims the free name. Aaron cannot claim a second name while he holds one.
Under each sentence is a call, and then what must be true afterwards. The answer. The event. The state. The spans in the trace.
You don't check the code. You read the sentences, and say yes, or no, or you've missed one.
Now the author has to prove something odd: that its journeys can fail.
ortho prove, with the flag empty, runs every journey on handlers that do nothing.
lines.say: Ortho prove, with the flag empty, runs every journey on handlers that do nothing.

lines.text: Seven journeys. Fifty-six steps. Fifty of them red.
That's the result you want. A check that can't fail proves nothing.
And every red line says what it expected. Expected: refused, with profile not found. Got: failed, with five hundred.
Six steps are green already, marked proved by the description. The blueprint says who may call, so the runtime refuses a stranger before any handler runs. Nobody has to build those.
So before a single handler exists, you hold two things. The stories, which you agreed. And a red run, which shows they bite.
Three things go wrong here. A journey that's green on the empty run, and isn't proved by the description, can't fail. Send it back.
An author who is also the builder writes down what the code does, not what you meant. Use two sessions.
And be plain about this one: nothing in Orthograph enforces that split for you yet. It's a way of working, and you keep it by how you hand out the work.
Next: a builder gets one brief, and climbs.
